title: Methodology & Limitations
text: This page documents how the three portfolio projects connect, and is intentionally direct about scope and limitations — knowing what a project doesn’t cover is as important as what it does.

title: Methodology & Limitations
text:
How the Three Projects Connect
The NASA RUL model’s predictions now feed directly into the Cost & ROI Optimization project. Each held-out test engine’s predicted RUL is converted into a failure-probability signal (1 - predicted_RUL / 125, clipped to [0,1]), which the cost-optimization framework consumes directly — rather than the two projects operating on independent simulated data. This makes the portfolio a genuine pipeline (classifier → business decision layer) rather than three standalone demos sharing a theme.
The Real-Time Sensor Dashboard remains a separate simulation of live telemetry streaming and alerting — it demonstrates the operational-monitoring layer of a PdM system, which is architecturally distinct from the offline RUL/ROI pipeline (a live dashboard reacts to streaming data; RUL/ROI here operate on batch, held-out historical data).

title: Methodology & Limitations
text:
Known Limitations

Single operating condition, single fault mode. FD001 represents one operating regime (sea level) and one fault mode (HPC degradation). A model trained here would need re-validation on FD002/FD004 (multiple operating conditions) before claiming applicability to more complex real-world fleets.
Small held-out test set for the cost-optimization framework. The connected ROI analysis draws on 100 held-out engines with only 16 true near-failures. The specific dollar figures and optimal threshold (\(\tau \approx 0.59\)) should be read as illustrative of the method, not as a production-ready dollar forecast — a real deployment would want a much larger fleet history before setting an operational threshold.
RUL-to-probability conversion is a simplifying heuristic. failure_probability = 1 - predicted_RUL / 125 is a reasonable but simple linear mapping. A more rigorous version would calibrate this conversion against actual observed failure rates at each predicted-RUL band, or use quantile regression to produce a genuine probabilistic estimate rather than a linear proxy.
No explicit group-leakage handling was needed here, since the CMAPSS train/test split is already provided pre-separated by engine — but it’s worth naming explicitly: a naive random k-fold split on this kind of engine-cycle data would leak information across train/test (adjacent cycles from the same engine landing on both sides), inflating validation scores in a way that wouldn’t hold up in deployment.
The cost matrix values ($1,500 / $300 / $10,000) are illustrative industry-typical figures, not sourced from a specific real fleet — a production version would calibrate these against actual historical maintenance and downtime costs for the specific asset class.

title: NASA Turbofan RUL Prediction
text:
NoteExecutive Summary



This project builds an end-to-end predictive maintenance pipeline using the NASA CMAPSS Turbofan Engine Degradation dataset (FD001). By applying rolling temporal feature engineering and training a LightGBM regressor, we forecast the Remaining Useful Life (RUL) of aircraft engines to enable proactive maintenance scheduling. Model performance is validated on the official held-out test set, not just training data.

title: NASA Turbofan RUL Prediction
text:
1. Data Ingestion & Target Preparation
We load raw telemetry from FD001 and calculate target Remaining Useful Life (RUL) labels. Target values are capped at 125 cycles to stabilize early-life training.


Code
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import lightgbm as lgb
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, mean_absolute_error, r2_score

# Set plot aesthetic
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")

# Define C-MAPSS column headers
index_names = ['unit_nr', 'time_cycles']
setting_names = ['setting_1', 'setting_2', 'setting_3']
sensor_names = [f's_{i}' for i in range(1, 22)]
col_names = index_names + setting_names + sensor_names

# Load raw training data
df_raw = pd.read_csv('../data/raw/train_FD001.txt', sep=r'\s+', header=None, names=col_names)

# Compute RUL target variable and clip at 125
max_cycles = df_raw.groupby('unit_nr')['time_cycles'].transform('max')
df_raw['RUL'] = max_cycles - df_raw['time_cycles']
df_raw['RUL'] = df_raw['RUL'].clip(upper=125)

# Feature Engineering: 5-cycle rolling mean
feature_cols = ['setting_1', 'setting_2', 's_2', 's_3', 's_4', 's_7', 's_8', 's_11', 's_12', 's_13', 's_15']
for col in feature_cols:
    df_raw[f'{col}_roll_mean'] = df_raw.groupby('unit_nr')[col].transform(lambda x: x.rolling(5, min_periods=1).mean())

all_feature_cols = feature_cols + [f'{col}_roll_mean' for col in feature_cols]
X_train = df_raw[all_feature_cols]
y_train = df_raw['RUL']

print(f"Training set prepared: {X_train.shape[0]} rows, {X_train.shape[1]} features")


Training set prepared: 20631 rows, 22 features

3. LightGBM Model Training
We fit a LGBMRegressor on our engineered rolling sensor features using standard hyperparameter baselines.


Code
# Initialize and train LightGBM regressor
model = lgb.LGBMRegressor(
    n_estimators=100,
    learning_rate=0.05,
    max_depth=5,
    random_state=42,
    verbose=-1
)

model.fit(X_train, y_train)

# In-sample prediction check
y_train_pred = model.predict(X_train)
rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_train, y_train_pred))
mae = mean_absolute_error(y_train, y_train_pred)
r2 = r2_score(y_train, y_train_pred)

print(f"Training Metrics -> RMSE: {rmse:.2f} | MAE: {mae:.2f} | R2: {r2:.2f}")


Training Metrics -> RMSE: 17.27 | MAE: 12.90 | R2: 0.83

title: NASA Turbofan RUL Prediction
text:
4. Held-Out Test Set Validation






ImportantWhy This Matters



The training metrics above are in-sample — computed on the same data the model learned from, which tends to look optimistic. To get an honest read on generalization, we evaluate on NASA’s official held-out test set (test_FD001.txt + RUL_FD001.txt) — 100 engines the model never saw during training, evaluated at the exact cycle the CMAPSS test protocol specifies.




Code
# Load the official held-out test set
df_test = pd.read_csv('../data/raw/test_FD001.txt', sep=r'\s+', header=None, names=col_names)

for col in feature_cols:
    df_test[f'{col}_roll_mean'] = df_test.groupby('unit_nr')[col].transform(lambda x: x.rolling(5, min_periods=1).mean())

# Ground truth: RUL at the LAST recorded cycle of each test engine
rul_truth = pd.read_csv('../data/raw/RUL_FD001.txt', header=None, names=['RUL'])
rul_truth['unit_nr'] = rul_truth.index + 1

# CMAPSS test protocol: predict RUL at the cutoff point of each sequence
df_test_last = df_test.groupby('unit_nr').tail(1).reset_index(drop=True)
df_test_last = df_test_last.merge(rul_truth, on='unit_nr')
df_test_last['RUL'] = df_test_last['RUL'].clip(upper=125)

X_test = df_test_last[all_feature_cols]
y_test = df_test_last['RUL']
y_test_pred = model.predict(X_test)

test_rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, y_test_pred))
test_mae = mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_test_pred)
test_r2 = r2_score(y_test, y_test_pred)

print(f"Held-Out Test Metrics -> RMSE: {test_rmse:.2f} | MAE: {test_mae:.2f} | R2: {test_r2:.2f}")


Held-Out Test Metrics -> RMSE: 17.87 | MAE: 12.58 | R2: 0.80




Code
def cmapss_score(y_true, y_pred):
    """Official CMAPSS asymmetric scoring function. Penalizes late
    (unsafe/optimistic) predictions more heavily than early
    (conservative) ones, matching real maintenance-scheduling risk -
    unlike plain RMSE, which treats both directions equally."""
    diff = np.asarray(y_pred) - np.asarray(y_true)
    score = np.where(diff < 0, np.exp(-diff / 13) - 1, np.exp(diff / 10) - 1)
    return float(np.sum(score))

test_cmapss = cmapss_score(y_test, y_test_pred)
print(f"CMAPSS asymmetric score: {test_cmapss:.2f} (lower is better)")


CMAPSS asymmetric score: 915.95 (lower is better)

See the Methodology & Limitations page for a full discussion of scope and constraints.

# Convert RUL prediction into a failure-probability signal, and save it
# so the Cost & ROI Optimization project can consume REAL model output
# instead of simulated data - connecting the two projects into one
# pipeline (classifier -> business decision layer).
df_test_last['predicted_RUL'] = y_test_pred

              'actual_failure_soon']].to_csv('../data/real_model_outputs_for_roi.csv', index=False)

title: NASA Turbofan RUL Prediction
text:
7. Executive Summary & Next Steps






TipBusiness Value



This pipeline enables condition-based maintenance scheduling, allowing operations teams to service engine units before failure occurs while maximizing overall component lifespan. Performance is validated on held-out engines, giving operations teams a defensible basis for scheduling decisions.


Key Model Takeaways * Primary Failure Drivers: Sensor 11 (s_11) and Sensor 4 (s_4) rolling means carry over 40% of overall model decision weight. * Validated Generalization: R² of 0.80 on 100 held-out engines the model never trained on, closely matching in-sample performance (R² 0.83) — indicating the model isn’t overfit.
Next Steps & Iterations * Multi-Condition Evaluation: Extend model training across NASA CMAPSS dataset variants with complex operating environments (FD002, FD004). * LSTM Architecture: Benchmark LightGBM performance against a Deep Learning Recurrent Neural Network (LSTM) to evaluate sequential memory gains. * See the Methodology & Limitations page for known constraints and scope.

title: E-Commerce A/B Test: New Landing Page Analysis
text:
ImportantExecutive Summary



An e-commerce company built a new landing page to increase conversions and ran an A/B test on 294,478 users. This project answers the real business question — ship it, keep the current page, or test longer — with the full statistical rigor that most A/B-test tutorials skip: data contamination handling, a sample-ratio-mismatch check, a confidence interval, and a power analysis distinguishing “no effect” from “not enough data.”

title: E-Commerce A/B Test: New Landing Page Analysis
text:
The Verdict
Do not ship the new page. The difference in conversion rate is not statistically significant (p = 0.905), and the 95% confidence interval for the difference spans zero. A power analysis confirms this null result is trustworthy — the test could reliably detect an effect as small as 0.35 percentage points, and the observed effect falls within the range it could not distinguish from noise.

title: E-Commerce A/B Test: New Landing Page Analysis
text:
Methodology

Data cleaning: 1.32% of rows had a mismatched group/page assignment (e.g. a “control” user who saw the new page) and were excluded, since their behavior can’t be attributed to either version. Duplicate user IDs were also removed, keeping the first occurrence.
Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM) check: verified the ~50/50 split was healthy (chi-square p=0.947) before trusting any downstream comparison.
Main test: one-sided two-proportion z-test (H1: new page conversion > old page conversion), with a 95% confidence interval for the absolute difference.
Power analysis: calculated the minimum detectable effect at 80% power given the actual sample size, to distinguish a genuine null result from an underpowered one.
Daily trend check: examined conversion rate by day across the 23-day test window to rule out a novelty effect.

title: E-Commerce A/B Test: New Landing Page Analysis
text:
Why This Project
Most A/B testing portfolio projects stop at “the p-value was above/below 0.05.” This one demonstrates the parts that separate a rigorous analyst from a p-value lookup: catching real data contamination before trusting a result, verifying randomization health via an SRM check, and correctly interpreting a null result by checking whether the test was even powered to detect a meaningful effect in the first place.

title: Predictive Maintenance ROI & Cost Optimization
text:
NoteExecutive Summary



Standard machine learning evaluation metrics like F1-score treat all misclassifications equally. In industrial predictive maintenance, however, a False Negative (missing a catastrophic breakdown) is exponentially more expensive than a False Positive (sending a technician on an unnecessary check).
This project constructs a custom financial optimization model that tunes classification decision boundaries (\(\tau\)) to minimize net operational expenditure (\(\text{OpEx}\)), applied to real predictions from the NASA Turbofan RUL model rather than simulated data.

title: Predictive Maintenance ROI & Cost Optimization
text:
1. Cost Matrix Definition
To align model performance with business goals, we define an asymmetric loss matrix based on typical industrial maintenance values:








Classification State
Real-World Scenario
Cost Penalty ($)




True Positive (TP)
Scheduled preventive maintenance performed before failure
$1,500


False Positive (FP)
Technician inspects asset; no defect found (False alarm)
$300


False Negative (FN)
Unplanned breakdown, secondary damage, emergency downtime
$10,000


True Negative (TN)
Healthy machine operates continuously without intervention
$0

title: Predictive Maintenance ROI & Cost Optimization
text:
2. Mathematical Optimization Framework
The total expected operational expense (\(\text{OpEx}\)) for a fleet of \(N\) assets is defined as:
\[\text{OpEx}(\tau) = (C_{\text{TP}} \cdot \text{TP}) + (C_{\text{FP}} \cdot \text{FP}) + (C_{\text{FN}} \cdot \text{FN}) + (C_{\text{TN}} \cdot \text{TN})\]
Where \(C_x\) represents the specific cost penalty, and predictions depend on threshold \(\tau\):
\[\hat{y} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } P(\text{Failure}) \ge \tau \\ 0 & \text{if } P(\text{Failure}) < \tau \end{cases}\]

title: Predictive Maintenance ROI & Cost Optimization
text:
3. Real Model Output & Threshold Optimization






NoteWhat Changed



The original version of this project used simulated failure probabilities (np.random.beta(...)) to demonstrate the cost-threshold framework. This version consumes real predictions from the NASA RUL model, connecting the two projects into a single pipeline: classifier output feeds directly into the business decision layer, rather than two independent demos sharing a theme. See Methodology & Limitations for how failure_probability is derived from predicted_RUL.




Code
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")

# Real model output, exported by the NASA RUL project's held-out
# test-set evaluation (see nasa-rul.qmd, Section 4).
df = pd.read_csv('../data/real_model_outputs_for_roi.csv')

y_true = df['actual_failure_soon'].values
y_probs = df['failure_probability'].values

# Define Cost Matrix
C_TP, C_FP, C_FN, C_TN = 1500, 300, 10000, 0

# Cost calculation function
def calculate_total_cost(y_true, y_probs, threshold):
    y_pred = (y_probs >= threshold).astype(int)
    tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred, labels=[0, 1]).ravel()
    total_cost = (tp * C_TP) + (fp * C_FP) + (fn * C_FN) + (tn * C_TN)
    return total_cost, tp, fp, fn, tn

# Sweep thresholds from 0.01 to 0.99
thresholds = np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 100)
cost_results = [calculate_total_cost(y_true, y_probs, t)[0] for t in thresholds]

# Identify optimal threshold
opt_idx = np.argmin(cost_results)
opt_threshold = thresholds[opt_idx]
min_cost = cost_results[opt_idx]

print(f"Fleet size (held-out test engines): {len(df)}")
print(f"Actual failures-soon in this fleet: {int(y_true.sum())}")
print(f"Optimal Threshold (tau): {opt_threshold:.2f}")
print(f"Minimum Total OpEx: ${min_cost:,.2f}")


Fleet size (held-out test engines): 100
Actual failures-soon in this fleet: 16
Optimal Threshold (tau): 0.59
Minimum Total OpEx: $27,600.00

title: Predictive Maintenance ROI & Cost Optimization
text:
6. Executive Key Results






TipBusiness ROI Summary



On a held-out fleet of 100 engines (16 true near-failures), shifting decision thresholds from the standard default (\(\tau = 0.50\)) to a cost-optimized threshold (\(\tau \approx 0.59\)) eliminates all missed failures while reducing total cost from $29,400 to $27,600.


Key Strategic Insights * Aggressive Failure Prevention: Raising \(\tau\) to the cost-optimal point eliminates all missed breakdowns (false negatives), where failure costs are \(33\times\) higher than inspection costs, at the expense of a modest increase in false alarms. * Directional Validation: Both strategies dramatically outperform a reactive run-to-failure policy ($160,000 total cost on this fleet), confirming the cost-optimization approach holds up on real model output, not just simulated data.






WarningReading These Numbers



This held-out fleet has only 100 engines and 16 true near-failures — enough to validate the method, but too small to treat the specific dollar figures or optimal threshold as a production-ready forecast. See Methodology & Limitations for details.


Next Steps & Implementation * Validate threshold stability on a larger fleet (e.g. combining FD001-FD004) before treating \(\tau \approx 0.59\) as an operational recommendation. * Integrate dynamic threshold tuning based on seasonal fluctuations in emergency repair labor costs. * Deploy automated notifications directly to field technicians when asset failure risk exceeds the optimized threshold.

Methodology
All aggregation is done in SQL, run directly against the raw CSVs via DuckDB — no spreadsheet or pandas pre-aggregation. The six core queries (headline KPIs, delivery-vs-review correlation, monthly trends, category risk, state performance, payment breakdown) are documented in full in the project’s GitHub repository.
Key definitions:

Only orders with status delivered are included in revenue/review figures.
“Late” is defined as delivered after the carrier’s own estimated delivery date.
Months with fewer than 100 orders (partial data at the start/end of the collection window) are excluded from trend charts to avoid misleading spikes.
Category and state breakdowns require at least 100 / 50 orders respectively to be included, to avoid small-sample noise.

title: Telco Customer Churn: Prediction & Retention Economics
text:
NoteExecutive Summary



This project goes beyond “train a churn classifier and report accuracy.” It answers a retention team’s actual question — not just who will churn, but what’s the dollar-optimal way to spend a limited retention budget on them — using real data from 7,043 telecom customers, RFM-style segmentation, a compared pair of models, and a per-customer cost-optimized decision threshold.

title: Telco Customer Churn: Prediction & Retention Economics
text:
Methodology
Two models — Logistic Regression and Random Forest — were trained on a stratified 75/25 train/test split and compared by ROC-AUC on the held-out set. The higher-AUC model’s predicted probabilities drive the cost-optimization analysis.
Unlike a flat cost matrix, each customer’s false-negative cost is their own annual revenue at stake (monthly charge × 12) — a more realistic model of what a retention team actually loses per missed churner, since losing a $30/month customer and a $100/month customer are not equally costly mistakes.
Customer segments were built via KMeans clustering on tenure (loyalty proxy), number of subscribed services (engagement proxy), and monthly charge (value proxy) — an RFM-style approach adapted for a subscription business rather than a transactional one.
Full SQL/Python source is in the project’s GitHub repository.

title: Telco Customer Churn: Prediction & Retention Economics
text:
Why This Project
Alongside the Olist BI Dashboard, this project rounds out the general-analytics side of this portfolio: churn prediction is one of the most common real-world classification problems across nearly every subscription or recurring-revenue business, and pairing a model with an explicit dollar-cost framework — rather than stopping at an accuracy score — is what makes a model’s output actionable to a non-technical stakeholder.
